rv.q: In his brilliant new play, however, he adds another weapon to his armoury.
‘Labour of Love’ is a big-hearted plea to remember what a progressive party can achieve when united.
This play is truly awwlll right, a rom-com pol-com that is knockabout funny and politically incisive.
What’s striking is just how coherent this up-to-the-minute response is.
He’s pulled it off again: Labour of Love is vastly enjoyable.
Jeremy Herrin’s production for his Headlong company in partnership with Michael Grandage’s outfit is as masterly as ever...
In its brightest moments this nearly three-hour show is an inventive hybrid of Much Ado About Nothing, Yes Minister and Stephen Sondheim’s Merrily We Roll Along.
To see Freeman and Greig on stage is a pleasure.
But Labour Of Love, while capturing a world with great success, is not in the same satirical class as the indelible Ink.
It’s not great comedy, but it’s a good play and perfectly performed.
His work not only brings recent history to thrilling life but he makes the monstrous egos of those drawn to this world, real, human, fallible and utterly compelling.
Put it on the ballot paper for Play of the Year!
It is a balancing act of considerable sophistication and skill – and it is absolutely wonderful.
James Graham is able to make the workings of politics and politicians both theatrically compelling and deeply human.
Funny and illuminating though it is, it doesn't quite pull off the Benedick/Beatrice love affair.
Labour of love? Hard labour more like.
For the rest, Labour of Love will feel like hard labour.

cn.t: Graham's political romcom cleverly interweaves Labour Party history with a witty will-they-won't-they relationship, earning praise for its smart writing and Freeman-Greig chemistry, though some find it loses Graham's usual sharp edge.

vr.q: the chemistry between them is wonderful
